title: A Striking New Fish Species Discovered in Amazon - Nautilus
gist: A new killifish, Laimosemion laranja, discovered in Amapá State in the Brazilian Amazon and described in Zoosystematics and Evolution, is found in just three forest pools over ~10 square miles and already meets IUCN endangered criteria due to deforestation, mining, urban expansion and plastic pollution.

insights.claim: The newly discovered killifish Laimosemion laranja was found in just three small forest pools covering about 10 square miles in Brazil's Amapá State.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Tiny ranges make species highly vulnerable to local land-use changes.
insights.quote: L. laranja has been found in just three small forest pools so far, covering an area of about 10 square miles

insights.claim: The fish's habitat is threatened by deforestation, mining, urban expansion and plastic pollution, so it meets IUCN criteria for endangered status.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Endangered listings can constrain mining and development in the Amazon region.
insights.quote: Its habitat is under threat from deforestation, mining, urban expansion, and plastic pollution.

insights.claim: Researchers argue that poorly explored but highly threatened Amazon areas still hold undiscovered species, and new discoveries can draw conservation attention.
insights.speaker: David Nield
entities: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte
insights.so_what: Biodiversity discovery is used as a lever for conservation policy.
insights.quote: to draw attention to the conservation of areas that are still poorly explored but highly threatened

insights.claim: The species was identified by body proportions, scale counts, skeletal features—notably eight scales in a row unique among close relatives—and mitochondrial DNA barcoding.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: DNA barcoding is a standard tool in biodiversity assessment.
